t: The birthday paradox: why 23 people are enough for a 50% match
desc: Work out why 23 people give a better-than-even chance that two share a birthday, by computing the probability that nobody does.
check: Why is the answer so much lower than most people expect?
Roughly what is the chance of a shared birthday among 70 people?
Among 23 people, what is the chance that someone shares YOUR birthday, and why is it so different?
a: What matters is pairs: 23 people form 253 pairs, and each pair is a chance for a match.
About 99.9%.
Only about 6% (1 - (364/365)²²), because that needs a match with one specific date rather than any pair matching.

t: Prove that √2 is irrational
desc: Learn the classic proof by contradiction that √2 can't be written as a fraction, then adapt it to other square roots and see exactly where it fails for perfect squares.
check: In the proof, why does a² = 2b² force both a and b to be even?
Where does the same argument break down if you try it on √4?
How do you adapt the proof to show √3 is irrational?
a: a² is even so a is even; write a = 2k, then 4k² = 2b² gives b² = 2k², so b is even too, contradicting a fraction in lowest terms.
a² = 4b² just gives a = 2b, a perfectly consistent solution, so no contradiction appears: √4 = 2/1.
If 3 divides a² then 3 divides a, because 3 is prime; the same chain of steps then shows 3 divides b.

t: The bridges of Königsberg: when can you draw a shape in one stroke?
desc: Learn Euler's solution to the Seven Bridges of Königsberg puzzle, the birth of graph theory, and the simple rule for when a figure can be traced without lifting your pen.
check: Why can't you cross each of Königsberg's 7 bridges exactly once?
Why must every graph have an even number of odd-degree vertices?
If a figure has exactly two odd-degree vertices, where must a one-stroke drawing start?
a: All four land masses touch an odd number of bridges, but a route using each edge once allows at most 2 odd-degree vertices (its start and end).
Each edge adds 2 to the total of all degrees, so that total is even, which forces the number of odd degrees to be even.
At one of the two odd vertices; the drawing will end at the other.

t: Why there are infinitely many primes, and roughly how many
desc: Learn Euclid's proof that the primes never run out, then the prime number theorem's estimate of how many primes lie below a given number and how far apart they are.
check: Is 2×3×5×7×11×13 + 1 prime? Why does Euclid's proof work either way?
Estimate how many primes there are below 1 million.
Roughly how big is the average gap between primes near 1 billion?
a: No: 30031 = 59 × 509. But none of its prime factors can be on the list, since dividing by any of them leaves remainder 1, so the list was incomplete.
About ln(10⁹) ≈ 21.

t: Bayes' theorem: why a positive test often means you're fine
desc: Learn Bayes' rule using natural frequencies (picture 1000 people), and apply it to medical screening, alarms and evidence.
check: A disease affects 1 in 1000 people. A test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific. If you test positive, what's the chance you're sick?
If a second, independent test also comes back positive, what's the chance now?
Why do false positives dominate when screening for rare conditions?
a: About 9%: per 1000 people there's ~1 true positive against ~10 false positives.
Even a small false-positive rate, applied to the huge healthy majority, produces more positives than the few real cases.

t: Why testing yourself beats rereading: spacing and retrieval practice
desc: Learn the forgetting curve, the testing effect and the spacing effect, then design a review schedule for something you actually want to remember.
check: Why does rereading feel effective but produce weaker memories than self-testing?
Why do longer gaps between reviews improve long-term retention?
Sketch a review schedule for 50 new words you must know in one month.
a: Rereading builds familiarity that feels like knowing; effortful recall strengthens the memory and exposes what you can't actually retrieve.
Some forgetting makes the next recall harder, and effortful recall consolidates memory more durably than repetition while it's still fresh.
Expanding gaps, e.g. test on days 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 28, moving easy words to longer gaps and keeping missed ones on short gaps.

t: The gambler's fallacy and why the casino always wins
desc: Learn independence, expected value and the law of large numbers, and why streaks don't 'balance out' while the house edge reliably adds up.
check: After 10 reds in a row on a fair roulette wheel, is black more likely on the next spin?
In European roulette (18 red, 18 black, 1 green zero), what's the expected loss per 100 bet on red?
Why doesn't the law of large numbers mean results 'even out'?
a: No: spins are independent, so the chance is still 18/37.
The proportion of reds approaches 18/37, but the absolute gap from the expected count typically grows like √n: it's diluted, not cancelled.

t: Cantor's diagonal argument: why some infinities are bigger than others
desc: Learn what it means for two infinite sets to be the same size, show that the fractions can be listed one by one, and prove that the real numbers cannot.
check: How can you list all positive fractions in a single infinite sequence?
Explain why any list of real numbers between 0 and 1 must miss at least one.
Are there more points on a 1 m line segment than on a 1 cm one?
a: Arrange p/q in a grid by numerator and denominator and zigzag along the diagonals, skipping duplicates; every fraction gets a finite position.
Build a number whose nth digit differs from the nth digit of the nth number listed (avoiding 0 and 9); it differs from every entry, so it's missing.
No: x → 100x pairs each point of one with exactly one point of the other, so they have the same cardinality.

t: Square any 2-digit number ending in 5 in under 3 seconds
desc: Learn the rule: for n5², multiply n by n+1 and append 25 (65²: 6×7 = 42, so 4225). Prove why it works with algebra, then drill 20 random cases.
check: You can square any number from 15 to 95 ending in 5 in under 3 seconds
You can show why (10n+5)² = 100n(n+1) + 25
You can extend it to 3-digit cases like 105² = 11025 and 115² = 13225

t: Calculate percentages instantly with the swap trick
desc: Learn that x% of y equals y% of x, plus the 10%, 5% and 1% building blocks, then drill tips, discounts and price increases on real prices.
check: You can do problems like 8% of 25 or 16% of 50 in under 5 seconds using the swap
You can compute a 15% or 18% tip on any bill under 200 in under 10 seconds
You can reverse a percentage (e.g. 64 after 20% off means the original was 80)

t: Estimate square roots in your head to 2 decimal places
desc: Learn the approximation √(n² + d) ≈ n + d/(2n) using the nearest perfect square, then drill it on random numbers and check each answer with a calculator.
check: You can estimate √50 ≈ 7.07 and √140 ≈ 11.83 in your head
Your estimates for 10 random whole numbers between 10 and 200 are all within 0.05 of the true value
You can explain why the estimate is best when d is small compared with n

t: Settle the Monty Hall problem with three cups and a coin
desc: With a friend as the host, hide a coin under one of three cups and play 30 rounds where you always stick and 30 where you always switch, then explain the result.
check: You recorded 60 rounds and switching won roughly twice as often as sticking
You can explain the answer using the 100-door version of the puzzle
You can explain why it matters that the host knows where the coin is and always reveals an empty cup

t: Multiply any two 2-digit numbers in your head
desc: Learn left-to-right cross multiplication (tens×tens, then the cross terms, then units×units) plus the near-100 shortcut, then drill 20 random problems.
check: You get at least 18 of 20 random 2-digit products right
Your average time is under 15 seconds per problem
You can do numbers just below 100 almost instantly, e.g. 97×94 = 9118

t: Build a memory palace and memorize 20 random words in order
desc: Pick 20 locations along a route through your home, generate 20 random words, place a vivid, exaggerated image of each word at one location, then test yourself.
check: You recall all 20 words in order straight afterwards
You recall at least 18 in order after 24 hours
You can recite the list backwards or name the 13th word directly

t: Compute logarithms in your head from three memorized numbers
desc: Memorize log₁₀ of 2, 3 and 7 (0.301, 0.477, 0.845), use log rules to get the logs of other numbers, and use them to estimate huge powers.
check: You can give log₁₀ of every whole number from 1 to 10 to 2 decimals without a calculator
You work out that 2⁶⁴ has 20 digits and starts with about 1.8
You can estimate log₁₀ of numbers like 3500 or 0.006 to within 0.01

t: Solve the 12-coin weighing puzzle
desc: One of 12 identical-looking coins is fake: either heavier or lighter. Using a balance scale only 3 times, find the fake and say whether it's heavy or light. Solve it before looking anything up.
check: You have a written strategy that handles all 24 possibilities
You can explain why 3 weighings give at most 27 distinguishable outcomes
You can argue why 14 coins could never be solved in 3 weighings

t: Learn the winning strategy for Nim using binary
desc: Learn to compute the nim-sum (the XOR of the pile sizes in binary) and always move to a position where it's zero. Then play against a friend or a Nim app.
check: You can compute the nim-sum of piles like 3, 5, 7 in your head
You win 5 games in a row whenever you start from a position with non-zero nim-sum
You can explain why every move from a zero nim-sum position produces a non-zero one

t: Name the weekday of any date with Conway's Doomsday rule
desc: Learn the Doomsday algorithm: the century anchors, the easy-to-remember dates (4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10, 12/12, 5/9, 9/5, 7/11, 11/7, last day of February) and the year formula.
check: You know 2026's doomsday is Saturday and can find the weekday of any 2026 date in under 10 seconds
You can do any date from 1900 to 2099 in under 30 seconds
You got 10 out of 10 random dates right, checked against a calendar

t: Memorize 50 digits of pi with the Major System
desc: Learn the Major System (each digit is a consonant sound: 0=s, 1=t/d, 2=n, 3=m, 4=r, 5=l, 6=j/sh, 7=k, 8=f/v, 9=p/b), turn digit pairs into words, and chain them into a story or memory palace.
check: You can turn any 2-digit number into a word in under 3 seconds
You recite the first 50 digits of pi without an error
You can still recite them the next day

t: Square any 2-digit number in your head in under 5 seconds
desc: Learn the method a² = (a-b)(a+b) + b², shifting to the nearest multiple of ten (47² = 44×50 + 3² = 2209), then drill until it's fast.
check: You get at least 19 of 20 random 2-digit squares right
Your average time is under 5 seconds per square
You can explain the algebra and use it for numbers like 98² = 9604 or 103² = 10609
